section_summary: This section documents U.S. concern over Japan’s acquisition of strategic materials—including mercury, steel, tetraethyl lead, copper, cobalt, arms, and petroleum—and debates over tightening export controls. It combines diplomatic and intelligence reporting with public and congressional correspondence advocating broader embargoes and greater aid to China. The final portion centers on British-American consideration of tanker controls to prevent Japan from enlarging its oil reserves, accompanied by detailed estimates of Japanese stocks, consumption, and shipping capacity.

subfiles.title: Continuation of confidential report on Japanese mercury requirements and purchases
subfiles.from: U.S. Army intelligence; signed Sherman Miles
subfiles.to: Department of State and other agencies
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese mercury consumption, reserve requirements, purchases, seizures, and possible international efforts to control the mercury market.
subfiles.summary: Report estimates a two-year Japanese mercury shortage and an Army-Navy goal of 10,000 flasks, half bought; Britain seized most of a 10,000-flask Nagara Maru shipment at Colombo, and Axis efforts to corner the market are assessed.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of telephone call concerning a rejected Japanese steel order
subfiles.about: Records Republic Steel’s rejection of a Japanese order for 30,000 tons of steel ingots.
subfiles.summary: Forrest Rutherford reports Japanese agents seeking large steel purchases after the scrap embargo; Republic Steel refused a 30,000-ton ingot order as conforming to U.S. foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese production of tetraethyl lead
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese research, production, and planned expansion of tetraethyl-lead manufacturing.
subfiles.summary: Source says Japan has no reserve of tetraethyl lead but secretly produces it and plans to expand after U.S. patent protection expires at the end of 1940.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s routing note to Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a letter for the Under Secretary.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary's note directing Hornbeck to prepare a letter for Welles, routing public correspondence on exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Delcevare King letter enclosing Major Eliot’s article on the Japanese embargo
subfiles.about: Urges a complete embargo on iron, steel, and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: King argues that Japan’s alliance with Germany and Italy makes continued American supply of war materials intolerable. The enclosed Major Eliot column criticizes loopholes permitting rails, finished steel, petroleum products, ships, and Philippine scrap to reach Japan and calls for either a total iron-and-steel embargo or none.

subfiles.title: Reply to Delcevare King on controls over scrap and ship sales
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains existing licensing restrictions on scrap exports and addresses concerns about rails and ships.
subfiles.summary: Allen tells Delcevare King all grades of iron and steel scrap are licensed, limited to the Western Hemisphere and Britain; used rails count as scrap, and no U.S.-registered vessels were recently sold to Japan for scrapping.

subfiles.title: Bessie C. Randolph letters supporting stronger Far Eastern measures
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull; enclosure addressed to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Commends current policy while advocating broader embargoes, aid to Britain, and possible naval use of Singapore.
subfiles.summary: Randolph praises restrictions on aviation gasoline and scrap steel but urges embargoes on copper, pig iron, motor vehicles, and Japanese imports to the United States. She also suggests considering American naval use of Singapore and warns that delay could make a later conflict with Japan more costly.

subfiles.title: Internal note on Bessie C. Randolph
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Comments on Randolph’s family background and expertise in international affairs.
subfiles.summary: Note describing Bessie Randolph as a prominent Roanoke Randolph and a serious student of international law.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Bessie C. Randolph
subfiles.about: Acknowledges her views on the Far East and aid to Great Britain.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Randolph for her letter to the President on Far Eastern policy and British aid and her favorable remarks.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Madrid on Japanese mercury purchases in Spain
subfiles.about: Reports unusually large Mitsubishi and Mitsui mercury purchases and their intended shipment from Vigo.
subfiles.summary: Madrid telegram: Mitsubishi bought 4,200 flasks and Mitsui 1,300 flasks of Spanish mercury, beyond normal purchases, to leave Vigo for transshipment at Lisbon or Rio.

subfiles.title: Telegram 971 from Vichy on Japanese efforts to buy French arms
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese requests for French arms, diplomatic subordination to Berlin, and related Franco-Japanese and Soviet-Japanese matters.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 971 from Vichy: Chauvel confirms Japan approached France for arms Germany could release; Japanese Embassy staff in Paris came under Berlin, and Japan offered to supply arms for Indochina.

subfiles.title: Memorandum and proposed clauses for Japanese copper contracts
subfiles.about: Submits proposed cancellation and national-defense clauses for contracts covering copper exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Proposed copper-contract clauses, cleared with Defense Commission officials: cancel prohibited exports, refund undelivered material, and allow rescission if copper is needed for U.S. or Chilean defense.

subfiles.title: Telegram 975 requesting notice to the War and Navy Departments
subfiles.about: Requests that the War and Navy Departments be informed of the preceding arms-purchase report.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 975 asks the Department to pass Telegram 971, on Japanese arms purchases in France, to the War and Navy Departments.

subfiles.title: Paul Monroe letter urging a comprehensive trade embargo
subfiles.about: Advocates extending the Japanese embargo to all war-related goods and all American commerce with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Paul Monroe, a friend of China and the Japanese people, urges an embargo on all munitions and war-useful materials and ultimately all trade with Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Paul Monroe
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Monroe’s recommendations on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Allen thanks Monroe for his spirit and assures him the issues receive constant consideration.

subfiles.title: Treasury referral of W. M. Prindle’s letter
subfiles.about: Forwards Prindle’s recommendations for greater assistance to China.
subfiles.summary: Treasury refers W. M. Prindle's letter requesting further aid to China to State for acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: W. M. Prindle letter on Japanese trade and aid to China
subfiles.about: Poses questions advocating expanded embargoes and stronger assistance to China.
subfiles.summary: Prindle asks whether Japan still freely buys basic war materials and argues its Axis alliance warrants broader restrictions and more aid to China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. M. Prindle
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Prindle’s questions concerning the Far East and international affairs.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton tells Prindle his Treasury letter was referred to State, which gives the international situation continuing attention.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Paul Linz on copper sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a firm’s request for guidance on sales of Chilean or Peruvian copper to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Paul Linz says Chilean or Peruvian copper owned by a Hungarian firm was partly sold to Mitsui; his company will drop further Japanese sales if State wishes, and Trueblood will refer it.

subfiles.title: Senator Lister Hill’s transmittal of Mary McCoy’s letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s concerns about strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Lister Hill transmits Alabama College correspondent Mary McCoy's letter on commodities and vehicles still exported to Japan.

subfiles.title: Mary McCoy letter questioning continued exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why numerous strategic materials and vehicles continue to reach Japan despite public support for embargoes.
subfiles.summary: McCoy lists copper, steel, lead, ferro-alloys, oil, gasoline and vehicles as possibly unrestricted exports and warns of Japanese naval power from her time in Japan.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Hill
subfiles.about: Provides export-control laws and proclamations for possible transmission to Mary McCoy.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the Export Control Act, presidential proclamations, regulations, White House announcements, and releases concerning scrap, aviation gasoline, and lubricating oil. He states that further restrictions remain under careful governmental consideration and returns McCoy’s letter.

subfiles.title: Senator Vandenberg’s referral of L. W. Fast’s information request
subfiles.about: Asks State to explain existing embargoes to a Michigan school superintendent.
subfiles.summary: Senator Vandenberg forwards L. W. Fast's letter and asks the Department for the precise information he seeks on embargoes on supplies to Japan.

subfiles.title: L. W. Fast letter requesting authoritative embargo information
subfiles.about: Requests reliable material specifying which exports to Japan are restricted.
subfiles.summary: Fast says a local group studying U.S.-Far East relations wants an exact list of items covered by American embargoes against Japan.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Vandenberg
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Vandenberg’s referral and encloses the reply sent to L. W. Fast.
subfiles.summary: Hull returns Fast's letter to Vandenberg with a copy of the Department's direct response.

subfiles.title: State Department explanation of export controls to L. W. Fast
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the licensing system and prohibitions governing exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen supplies the National Defense Act, relevant proclamations and regulations, and White House releases. He explains that aviation gasoline, lubricating oil, and iron and steel scrap may be exported only to the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain, while other listed items remain subject to licensing based on U.S. defense needs.

subfiles.title: Warren A. Seavey letter transmitting criticism of Far Eastern policy
subfiles.about: Forwards Seavey’s letter to Roosevelt advocating stronger action toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Seavey sends Hull a copy of his letter to the President criticizing Far Eastern policy, believing Hull sympathizes.

subfiles.title: Warren A. Seavey letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Calls for a wider Japanese embargo, more aid to China, and joint Anglo-American control of Asian bases.
subfiles.summary: Citing an Alsop and Kintner article on a State Department division, Seavey argues public opinion permits stronger measures and delay makes Japan's southern expansion harder to reverse.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Warren A. Seavey
subfiles.about: Rejects claims of factions within the State Department while acknowledging legitimate differences of opinion.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that policy formulation is not obstructed by cliques or factional disputes. He characterizes differences among officers as healthy variations of approach in a democratic organization and encloses remarks from his October 8 press conference. He also confirms that Seavey’s Far Eastern recommendations have been carefully noted.

subfiles.title: Representative Jenkins’s referral of Eleanor Brooks’s postcard
subfiles.about: Requests that embargo information be furnished to Eleanor Brooks.
subfiles.summary: Representative Jenkins forwards Eleanor Brooks's postcard asking for documents on the Japanese embargo, to be sent to her directly.

subfiles.title: Eleanor Brooks postcard requesting embargo documents
subfiles.about: Requests the National Defense Act and legal materials governing scrap and aviation-gasoline embargoes.
subfiles.summary: Brooks asks for the National Defense Act and regulations restricting scrap and aviation gasoline.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Representative Jenkins
subfiles.about: Confirms that the requested embargo documents were sent to Eleanor Brooks.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Jenkins copies of the National Defense Act and scrap and aviation-gasoline regulations were sent to Brooks, and returns her postcard.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Eleanor Brooks
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Supplies the requested laws and policy announcements concerning exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen sends Brooks the National Defense Act, petroleum regulations, the September steel-scrap announcement and the July aviation-gasoline release.

subfiles.title: H. K. Masters memorandum on a cobalt shipment intended for Japan
subfiles.about: Warns that cobalt-bearing residues consigned to Mitsui and Mitsubishi could supply nearly a year of Japanese requirements.
subfiles.summary: Masters reports the Westhumhaw carried 462 tons of cobalt residues for Mitsui and 105 for Mitsubishi to the U.S.; unlicensed cobalt could be freely re-exported to Japan.

subfiles.title: Chinese Ambassador’s compliments slip
subfiles.about: Presents the accompanying texts of Hu Shih’s speeches.
subfiles.summary: Chinese Ambassador's compliments slip covering printed addresses by Hu Shih.

subfiles.title: “Saving Democracy in China” broadcast
subfiles.to: New York Herald Tribune Forum audience
subfiles.about: Argues that supporting China and Britain is essential to the worldwide defense of democracy.
subfiles.summary: Hu Shih's broadcast sees the scrap embargo, draft registration and Burma Road reopening as signs China and Britain face one aggression, and urges aid to both and a postwar enforceable peace.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of “Saving Democracy in China”
subfiles.to: New York Herald Tribune Forum audience
subfiles.about: Duplicates Hu Shih’s appeal for American support of China and Britain against Axis aggression.
subfiles.summary: This is a second copy of the broadcast printed on pages 210–213. It connects American defense measures and the reopening of the Burma Road to the common struggle against Japan, Germany, and Italy, and calls for American aid and postwar leadership.

subfiles.title: “China Fights” address
subfiles.about: Explains China’s endurance in the war against Japan and why China cannot accept a negotiated surrender.
subfiles.summary: Hu surveys China’s territorial losses, disrupted universities, severed trade routes, and reliance on the reopened Burma Road, while emphasizing China’s space, population, historic unity, agrarian resilience, industrial relocation, and foreign aid. He argues that surrender would destroy Chinese independence, compares China’s struggle to Valley Forge, and rejects appeasement through the example of Munich. China’s continued resistance, he concludes, prevents Japan from more fully assisting Germany and Italy in the global struggle against democracy.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s note requesting a meeting with Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Asks Hornbeck to arrange an office meeting upon his return.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary asks Hornbeck to meet in his office on his return about the British communication on Japanese oil imports.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum to Welles on the British oil communication
subfiles.about: Calls attention to an important British Embassy communication and recommends an early conference.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says copies of the British oil communication went to Atherton, Dunn and Hamilton and suggests Welles convene a conference promptly.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs outline of the British tanker-control proposal
subfiles.about: Summarizes and evaluates the British proposal for coordinated restrictions on tankers carrying oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs outlines the British proposal to deny Allied and U.S.-controlled tankers to Japan and restrict shipments via Dairen, Indochina and Thailand, with Navy verification of consumption figures.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck note to Hamilton concerning the British papers
subfiles.about: Requests recommendations on handling the British oil papers and their policy issue.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck asks Hamilton how to dispose of the British papers and what action to take on the substance.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter transmitting the Japanese oil-stock memorandum
subfiles.about: Transmits three copies of a memorandum on Japanese oil stocks and proposes consideration of controls on non-Japanese tankers.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy asks Hornbeck to share its Japanese oil-stock memorandum with Treasury and others, re-examine the estimates, and give U.S. views on limiting Japan's chartering of Allied tankers.

subfiles.title: Secret British statement on Japanese oil imports and joint tanker restrictions
subfiles.about: Proposes joint British-American action to restrict Japan’s use of non-Japanese tankers if revised calculations show continuing stock accumulation.
subfiles.summary: Secret British statement questions U.S. estimates of Japanese oil consumption, suggests stocks may exceed 5.25 million tons, and proposes joint refusal of tanker licenses and restrictions on Dairen, Indochina and Thailand shipments.

subfiles.title: “Japan: Oil Shipments and Tanker Control”
subfiles.about: Compares British and American estimates of Japanese oil consumption and calculates the effect of denying foreign-flag tanker capacity.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum disputes U.S. Navy estimates of Japanese oil use, calculates Japanese tanker capacity at about four million tons annually, and says denying foreign tankers could cut imports or stocks by up to 1.2 million tons.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck letter requesting Admiral Stark’s confidential review
subfiles.about: Sends the British oil memorandum to the Chief of Naval Operations for informal review and comment.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck sends Admiral Stark the British Embassy memorandum for confidential review, asking a Navy staff member to contact him informally before formal comment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese purchases in Brazil
subfiles.about: Points to a Justice Department letter reporting unusually large Japanese purchases in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: several sources report substantial Japanese purchases in Brazil, notably castor seed far above normal.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation concerning the Greek ship Olga E. Embericos
subfiles.about: Records naval intelligence concerning a Greek vessel carrying scrap steel to Japan despite crew objections.
subfiles.summary: Navy relays that the Greek ship Olga E. Embericos loaded about 8,300 tons of scrap at Boston and New York for Japan; the crew objected, but customs papers were in order, and the Navy referred it to State.
